title: Lottery Tax by State: What Winners Keep in 2026
description: Win a $500M Powerball jackpot? See exact take-home amounts after federal and state taxes for every major state — dollar figures, ranked best to worst.
content:
What This Article Calculates and Why Your State Determines Your Real Prize

If you won a $500 million Powerball jackpot tonight, here is exactly what you would take home in each state. Not a rough estimate. Not a percentage range. Specific dollar amounts, calculated step by step, showing how federal taxes hit first and your state's rate finishes the job. The difference between winning in Florida versus winning in New York is not academic — it is worth more than $27 million in real, spendable money.

Understanding lottery tax by state is the single most important financial calculation any jackpot winner can make before signing their ticket. This article walks through every number, starting with the federal burden, moving through the lump sum versus annuity decision, and landing on a ranked table of exactly what winners keep in every major state. Use our lottery tax calculator to run your own figures once you understand the methodology below.

Federal Tax Calculation: How the IRS Takes 37% Before Your State Gets Its Cut

Federal taxes hit every lottery winner the same way regardless of which state they live in. The process works in two stages, and both stages cost you money.

Stage 1: Mandatory 24% Withholding at Payout

The moment you claim a prize over $5,000, the lottery withholds 24% for federal taxes automatically. On a $248 million lump sum cash value (more on that figure in the next section), that withholding equals $59.52 million taken immediately. You receive a check for roughly $188.48 million and a tax form for the rest.

Stage 2: The Additional 13% Due at Tax Time

Withholding is not your final federal tax bill. As a single filer, any income above $626,350 falls into the 37% federal bracket in 2026. A lottery jackpot lands you firmly in that bracket for the entire lump sum amount. Since you already paid 24% at withholding, you owe an additional ~13% when you file your return. On a $248 million lump sum, that additional bill comes to roughly $32.24 million.

Total federal tax on the lump sum: approximately $91.76 million, leaving you with roughly $156.24 million before your state collects anything. This calculation assumes single-filer status and no deductions that would meaningfully reduce taxable income at this income level. Consult a tax professional for your specific situation.

Lump Sum vs. Annuity: Real Dollar Figures on a $500M Jackpot

Before state taxes enter the picture, you face the most consequential choice of your winner's life: take the lump sum cash option or accept the annuity paid over 29 years.

The Lump Sum Option

The advertised $500 million jackpot pays a lump sum cash value of approximately $248 million — roughly 60% of the headline number. After the full federal tax burden of 37%, that lump sum becomes approximately $156.24 million before state taxes. In a no-tax state, that is your final number. In a high-tax state like New York, state taxes reduce it further.

The Annuity Option

The annuity pays the full $500 million over 29 annual installments, with each payment increasing by 5% per year. The first payment is roughly $7.5 million; the final payment approximately $30 million. Each annual payment is taxed as ordinary income in the year received, so you pay federal and state taxes each year. While the annuity delivers more gross dollars over time, each payment still faces the 37% federal rate because even a single annual installment exceeds the top bracket threshold.

Most financial planners note that the annuity's total after-tax value versus the lump sum depends heavily on investment returns you could achieve with the lump sum. This article focuses on the lump sum for direct state-by-state comparison purposes, as it is the more commonly chosen option.

The difference between winning in New York versus Florida on a $500 million Powerball jackpot is more than $27 million in take-home pay — determined entirely by your zip code, not your ticket.

The Best and Worst States for Lottery Winners: Dollar-Amount Rankings

The Best States: Nine Jurisdictions Where Winners Keep the Most

Nine states and one commonwealth effectively charge lottery winners $0 in state income tax on a $248 million lump sum, leaving approximately $156.24 million after federal taxes:

  • California — State law explicitly exempts lottery winnings from state income tax
  • Florida — No state income tax of any kind
  • Texas — No state income tax of any kind
  • Washington — No state income tax of any kind
  • Wyoming — No state income tax of any kind
  • South Dakota — No state income tax of any kind
  • Tennessee — No state income tax on wages or winnings
  • New Hampshire — No broad-based state income tax
  • Pennsylvania — State law exempts lottery winnings from the state income tax

The Worst States: Where Winners Lose the Most to State Taxes

At the bottom of the rankings, New York City residents face the most punishing combined tax rate in the country. The state's 10.9% rate already costs winners $17.03 million on a $248 million lump sum. Add New York City's additional 3.876% local income tax — which applies to all NYC residents — and the combined state-plus-city rate reaches 14.776%, costing an additional $23.09 million and leaving NYC winners with approximately $133.11 million.

That is a gap of more than $23 million compared to a winner in the same state living outside city limits, and more than $27 million less than a winner claiming the same ticket in Florida or Texas. New Jersey and Washington D.C. follow at 10.75%, costing winners nearly $16.8 million each in state-level taxes alone.

For Mega Millions jackpots, the same state tax rates apply — only the federal math changes if the advertised jackpot size is different. The state-by-state ranking holds regardless of which game you play. Explore all state lottery guides for details specific to your location.

How to Calculate Your Own Lottery Taxes: Internal Tool Link and Methodology

The calculations in this article follow a straightforward four-step methodology you can apply to any jackpot size:

  1. Find the lump sum cash value. Multiply the advertised jackpot by approximately 0.60 to get the cash option payout.
  2. Apply the full federal tax rate. Multiply the cash value by 0.37 to find total federal taxes owed. Subtract from the cash value to get your pre-state amount.
  3. Apply your state's lottery tax rate. Multiply the pre-state amount by your state's rate. Subtract to get your post-state amount.
  4. Apply any local taxes. If you live in New York City, add the 3.876% city tax on top of the state rate before calculating.

For a personalized calculation that accounts for your specific filing status, deductions, and state, use our lottery tax calculator. It applies current 2026 federal brackets and all state-specific rates automatically. The methodology above uses the top marginal federal rate of 37% applied to the full lump sum. In practice, only income above $626,350 is taxed at 37%, meaning a small portion of a large jackpot technically falls in lower brackets — but on a $248 million lump sum, the blended effective rate is so close to 37% that the simplified calculation is accurate for planning purposes.
